title: Cupertino
name: Cupertino
metaTitle: Cupertino 1031 Exchange Investors | San Jose, CA
metaDescription: 1031 exchange guidance for Cupertino investors weighing Apple-adjacent NNN buildings, Stevens Creek Boulevard retail, and the slow-moving Vallco redevelopment.

sections.html: Cupertino is a small city where one company's footprint touches nearly every commercial parcel, and that concentration cuts both ways for an exchanger. Apple Park anchors real value in everything nearby, but a city this size with this little available land also means every parcel gets bid up on the assumption that proximity alone justifies the price. That imbalance rarely corrects on its own — a city this constrained on land tends to see pricing detach further from fundamentals the longer the cycle runs, not less.

sections.heading: Apple's Footprint Inflates Everything Nearby, Including the Risk
sections.html:
Apple Park and the company's older campuses along De Anza Boulevard and Stevens Creek Boulevard give Cupertino a name-brand identity that few small cities carry, and that identity shows up directly in asking prices for anything within walking distance.

The risk is that 'near Apple' becomes a substitute for actual underwriting. A retail pad or small office building priced on proximity rather than its own tenant roster and lease terms is a bet on continued corporate presence, and Cupertino's small footprint means there's little room to diversify away from that single dependency.

sections.heading: The Short List a Land-Starved City Actually Supports
sections.html:
Cupertino's limited land base narrows the realistic shortlist to a handful of product types:

  • small-footprint retail and office along Stevens Creek Boulevard and De Anza Boulevard
  • single-tenant NNN buildings leased to tech or service tenants near the Apple campuses
  • mixed-use residential and retail tied to the Vallco-area redevelopment
  • De Anza College-adjacent student and faculty-serving retail
  • a small stock of older office converted from pre-Apple Park uses

sections.heading: Vallco's Redevelopment Has Moved Slower Than the Renderings Suggest
sections.html:
The former Vallco Shopping Mall site has been through more than one redevelopment plan, and the project now known as The Rise represents years of entitlement work before ground actually moved. That timeline is worth remembering for any exchanger pricing a nearby parcel on the assumption that a large mixed-use project finishes on schedule.

Confirm the actual construction status and phasing directly with the city or the developer's public filings before treating a redevelopment story as priced-in value.

sections.heading: Land Scarcity Means Comps Age Quickly
sections.html:
Cupertino simply doesn't have much land left to develop, and that scarcity means a comparable sale from even a year or two back can already be stale. A broker citing an older transaction as the basis for today's asking price may be pointing to a market that has already moved.

An exchanger should pull the most recent closed comps available, not the most convenient ones, particularly for the smaller commercial parcels that make up most of what actually trades here. This matters most for the smaller parcels near Stevens Creek Boulevard, where a handful of recent sales can move the going rate more than a broker's general sense of the market.

sections.heading: Small Deal, Same Clock
sections.html:
A Cupertino property this concentrated around a single corporate presence needs the qualified intermediary, the tax advisor, and a lender who has reviewed the tenant roster directly, all working from the same file before identification.

Wait too long and the risk shows up fast: a lender questions the concentration, or a Vallco-area unit's redevelopment timeline shifts again, and the 180-day window closes with the gain still due. Confirm figures and deadlines with your own advisors; this page describes the market, not tax advice.

faqs.q: Does proximity to Apple Park justify a Cupertino price premium?
faqs.a: Only if the building's own tenant roster and lease terms support it. Proximity alone isn't underwriting.

faqs.q: Is Vallco-area redevelopment already priced into nearby parcels?
faqs.a: Confirm the project's actual construction status directly. Large mixed-use redevelopments here have taken years longer than initial plans suggested.

faqs.q: How current do my Cupertino comps need to be?
faqs.a: As current as possible. Land scarcity here means even a two-year-old comp can already understate today's pricing.

faqs.q: How many replacement properties am I allowed to name on my identification notice?
faqs.a: Up to three regardless of value under the standard rule, or more under the 200% rule if combined value stays within twice what you sold.

faqs.q: What happens if my Cupertino identification falls through near Day 45?
faqs.a: Have a genuinely underwritten backup ready and avoid taking receipt of exchange funds while you resolve it.

faqs.q: Should I expect large single-tenant campuses to trade often in Cupertino?
faqs.a: Rarely. Most large Apple-adjacent parcels stay under long-term corporate control, so the realistic opportunity for most exchangers sits in the smaller retail and office buildings nearby, not the campuses themselves.

faqs.q: Does De Anza College proximity support standalone retail demand?
faqs.a: To a degree, for student- and faculty-serving formats like cafes and services, but that demand is narrower than general retail traffic and should be underwritten on its own terms.

faqs.q: How should I treat a Cupertino building's age relative to Apple Park's construction era?
faqs.a: Confirm whether the building predates or postdates the current Apple campus, since older stock nearby was often built for a very different scale of tenant than what leases there today.

faqs.q: Are Cupertino lease terms typically longer than in neighboring cities?
faqs.a: Not automatically, and length alone isn't the point — what matters is whether the specific lease's renewal options, escalations, and remaining term line up with your hold period, which a broker's general market summary won't tell you.

faqs.q: Should I expect the same buyer competition on every Cupertino listing?
faqs.a: No. Smaller, well-priced parcels near the city center tend to draw more competing offers than larger or less central properties, so ask your broker for actual offer counts on comparable recent closings.
